title: Lab results portal
like: a patient portal that shows blood test results
brief: Labs send results to a portal, patients get a notice that a result is ready and open it. When the notice goes to thousands of people at the same minute, they all open the portal at once. Nobody should get the same notice twice.

clarify.q: How fast must a notice go out?
clarify.a: Within a few minutes of the result arriving. It can wait a little, but never be sent twice.

clarify.q: Do many patients open the portal at the same time?
clarify.a: Yes. A weekday 7 am batch of results notifies thousands at once, and about ten times the normal traffic arrives within a minute.

clarify.q: Can the queue ever deliver a message twice?
clarify.a: Yes, queues occasionally deliver the same message again, about 1 in 100 here. The notice step has to cope.
Partner labs, through an approved connection.

notes: A "write" is a lab sending a result in.
A "report" is a clinic printing a monthly summary.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

hints: Most traffic is reading the same result list again and again. What remembers an answer for a minute?
Notices are not urgent but must not repeat. A queue holds them; something must remember which ones have gone out.
Put an idempotency store next to the worker that sends the notice, then send through push and email providers.

editorial.summary: Three simple ideas make this a solid small system: a cache for the repeated reads, a queue for the notices that can wait, and an idempotency store so a repeated queue message does not become a repeated notice.

designs.name: Cached views, queue and a once-only notice
designs.why: Servers in two zones sit behind a load balancer; a short cache answers repeated result views; the SQL database stores results. Notices go through a queue to a worker, which asks the idempotency store whether this notice was already sent.

tradeoffs: A 60-second cache keeps the database calm in the rush and means a brand-new result can take up to a minute to appear for a patient who already looked.
The idempotency store costs about $100 a month and removes the one embarrassing failure: a patient getting the same alert three times.
Two notice channels (push and email) cost a little more and give you a fallback when one is slow.
The queue absorbs the 7 am wave of notices; the cost is that the last patients in the wave get theirs a minute later.
editorial.realWorld: Patient portals commonly see their daily peak just after results are released, and queues in most managed services deliver at least once, meaning a duplicate now and then is normal (approx.). Receiving the same alert twice is among the top complaints about notification systems.

correctness.prompt: A worker sends a message, then crashes before recording success. What key and delivery states would you store so a retry does not send it twice?
correctness.discussion: Give each logical message a stable key, scoped to its recipient and channel, and enforce a unique constraint on that key. Save the request and an outbox entry in one transaction, then track pending, sending and delivered states. A queue alone does not prevent duplicates. If the provider accepts the send but the worker crashes, retry with the same provider idempotency key or query its status. Without provider support, exactly-once external delivery cannot be guaranteed: discuss whether a possible duplicate or a possible missed message is acceptable.

fields.label: The provider accepts the operation, then the worker crashes before saving success. What state is durable?
options: Unknown outcome, with the original logical operation key
Failed, so the retry gets a new key
fields.explanation: Missing local success does not prove the provider rejected the operation.

fields.label: The queue redelivers that operation. What can establish one external effect?
options: Check a local cache, then send without a provider key
Reuse the provider idempotency key or reconcile its recorded outcome
fields.explanation: A local lookup and a remote side effect are not atomic. Without endpoint support, one external effect cannot be guaranteed; report uncertainty and choose an explicit recovery policy.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 175 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $8839. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
